title: Federal Judge Blocks New York's Ban on ICE Agents Wearing Masks
excerpt: The ruling follows similar judicial defeats for mask bans in California and other blue states, as the DOJ challenges Democratic resistance to Trump-era immigration enforcement.
body:
• A federal judge blocked New York's ban on ICE agents wearing masks and its requirement that agents display visible identification, ruling both provisions likely unconstitutional.
  • Judge Mae D'Agostino said only the federal government can establish policies governing federal law enforcement operations, echoing a similar ruling that struck down California's mask ban in February.
  • Governor Kathy Hochul and AG Letitia James said they are reviewing all legal options, calling masked agents a threat to community safety.
  • A separate provision barring local police from entering 287(g) cooperation agreements with ICE was left intact.

The Ruling

U.S. District Judge Mae D'Agostino of the Northern District of New York on Monday issued a preliminary injunction blocking two key provisions of a state law that would have prohibited federal immigration agents from wearing masks and required them to display visible identification while performing their duties.

https://x.com/GuntherEagleman/status/2084395819726143646

In her ruling, D'Agostino found that the challenged provisions were likely unconstitutional because they interfere with federal law enforcement operations — not just those carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, but also the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

"New York cannot impose its own uniform requirements on federal agents simply because it disagrees with how the Federal Government is exercising its authority."

— Judge Mae D'Agostino, U.S. District Court

How the Law Came About

New York's restrictions were enacted as part of the state's 2027 budget deal, signed by Governor Kathy Hochul in late June. The law reflected growing tensions between Democratic states and the Trump administration over immigration enforcement tactics, particularly ICE agents conducting operations while wearing balaclavas or face coverings.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cL5YOjDrET4

Beyond the mask ban and identification requirement, the law barred ICE from entering schools, healthcare facilities, and homes without judicial warrants. It also prohibited local law enforcement agencies from entering into 287(g) agreements — formal cooperation pacts that allow police to be deputized as immigration agents.

The Department of Justice filed suit within days of the law's enactment, calling it an illegal attempt to regulate the federal government. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche argued that the law threatened officers who "risk their lives every day," adding that New York's "anti-law enforcement policies are designed to create risk for our agents."

A Pattern Across Blue States

The ruling follows a now-familiar pattern. California, New Jersey, and Connecticut have all passed similar laws restricting ICE agents from wearing masks, and the DOJ has challenged each one. A federal judge struck down California's ban in February, ruling that it "unlawfully discriminates against federal officers."

New York lawmakers had argued their version would survive legal challenge because it applied to all law enforcement officers, not just federal agents. D'Agostino disagreed, finding that the practical effect still amounted to federal overreach.

What Survived

Notably, the judge declined to block the provision barring New York local law enforcement from entering 287(g) agreements with ICE. Several counties currently operate under such agreements, with a late-August deadline to terminate them. Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault said his county's agreement had resulted in nine individuals turned over to federal authorities since 2018.

What Comes Next

Governor Hochul and Attorney General James issued a joint statement pushing back on the ruling. "We stand firm in our belief that masked agents do not make New York safer," they said, adding that their offices are "reviewing all legal options."

For the Indian community — particularly those on work visas or navigating the immigration system — the ruling is the latest in a series of developments that have heightened anxiety around enforcement operations. Immigration attorneys have already advised H-1B holders and other visa holders to carry documentation at all times, even during domestic travel, as ICE operations expand in scope and visibility across the country.
